title: Content (Philippians 4:11–13)
hook: I have learned to be content, and I can do all things in him

segments.voice: Yesterday, arete: whatever is true, whatever lovely, think on these things. Your line was think on these.

I can do all things. It turns up on gym shirts, on locker-room walls, under an athlete's eyes in black grease paint. There it reads like a promise of winning: with God's help I'll make the team, close the deal, run the marathon. Read in place, it's something quieter. It comes near the end of a thank-you note. The church at Philippi had sent Paul a gift in prison, carried by a friend named Epaphroditus. And Paul, thanking them, says something surprising about needing it.
screen: `I CAN DO ALL THINGS: ON A GYM SHIRT.` → `READ IN PLACE: A THANK-YOU NOTE.` → `A GIFT SENT TO A PRISONER.`

segments.voice: He's glad of the gift, but he doesn't want them to think he was desperate: "Not as it were for want. For I have learned, in whatsoever state I am, to be content therewith." Then he names the states. He knows how to be brought low and how to abound; to be full and to be hungry; to have plenty and to go without. And he says he's been instructed in all of it. The Greek word is the one used for being initiated into a secret. Paul has learned the secret of being content. Then: "I can do all things in him who strengtheneth me." All things, here, means both: hunger and plenty, prison and freedom. Not winning, but standing steady through either. The word for content is autarkēs, and it's borrowed. It was an ideal the Stoic and Cynic philosophers prized: self-sufficient, needing nothing outside yourself. Paul takes their word and changes its center. Not sufficient in myself, but sufficient in him. And notice the first verb: I have learned. Contentment, for Paul, isn't a personality type. It's a skill, and it took practice, and he learned it in some very hard places. Catholic teaching on the tenth commandment speaks of the same freedom: a heart that isn't ruled by envy or by the need for more, which the Catechism calls poverty of heart. And Paul doesn't despise the gift either. He calls it a sweet fragrance, a sacrifice pleasing to God. Content doesn't mean ungrateful. It means grateful, without being owned.
screen: `NOT AS IT WERE FOR WANT.` · `BROUGHT LOW, AND ABOUNDING.` · `AUTARKĒS: SUFFICIENT, BUT IN HIM.` · `CONTENTMENT IS LEARNED.` · then, large: `I CAN DO ALL THINGS IN HIM WHO STRENGTHENETH ME.`

segments.voice: Look around wherever you are and quietly name five things that are here: a chair holding you up, light, your breath, a sound, a person or the memory of one. Don't name what's missing; let what's here be enough, and if a want shows up, let it pass by. If you pray, say today's verse slowly; if not, simply rest in what's already here.
Content. Paul's word from prison: I have learned, in whatever state I am, to be content, because I can do all things in him who strengthens me. Today's word.
Your line: I have learned. Contentment is a skill, not a mood. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Catholic teaching on the tenth commandment commends "poverty of heart" and freedom from envy and greed; Catholics practice contentment through simplicity, fasting and almsgiving.
